opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When people talk about "AI for AI," meaning using AI systems to accelerate AI research itself, I think China is in an interesting position.

There's a lot of energy right now. Many young researchers, both in universities and at companies, are taking seriously the idea that AI can automate parts of the research loop: generating hypotheses, writing and running experiments, reading the literature, even proposing new architectures. China has a few real advantages here. There's a large pool of talented, very hardworking engineers. Iteration is fast. And there's a strong culture of open-sourcing models, which lowers the barrier for everyone to build agents and tools on top of them.

My own perspective comes from a slightly different angle. I've spent a lot of time on what I call "physics of AI," treating neural networks almost like natural phenomena we can study scientifically, and on making models more interpretable, like with KANs. So when I think about AI for AI, my hope is that it isn't only about brute-force automation, running a million experiments and picking the best number. That can work, but it doesn't necessarily give us understanding. What excites me more is AI that helps us discover principles: why certain architectures work, what's actually happening inside the model, which laws govern training dynamics. If AI can help us do science on AI, not just engineering, that's a much bigger leap.

There's also a risk I see, not specific to China but maybe amplified by the speed there: everyone chasing the same benchmarks and the same leaderboard. AI for AI could make that worse, because it's very good at optimizing a metric you hand it. So the people who'll make a real difference are the ones who ask good questions and choose the right things to measure. Taste still matters a lot, maybe even more when execution becomes cheap.

Overall I'm optimistic. I think China will be one of the main places where this happens. The interesting question is whether we use it to go faster on the same road or to find new roads.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI for AI in China, but does not say it gained popularity shortly after Recursive's announcement.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think it's quite interesting, and honestly a bit surprising, how fast AI for Science has become a thing in China. A few years ago, when I was still an undergrad at Peking University, "AI for Science" wasn't really a phrase people used. If you were in physics, you did physics; if you were in computer science, you did computer science. The two communities barely talked to each other. Now you see dedicated institutes, big funding programs, companies like DP Technology, and a lot of young students who explicitly want to work at this intersection. That shift happened really quickly.

I think there are a few reasons. One is that China has a very strong tradition in the physical sciences and in applied mathematics, so there's a huge pool of people who already understand the domain problems. Once the tools became accessible, these people could pick them up fast. Another is that there's a kind of top-down push. When the government says this is a priority direction, resources move very quickly, much faster than in the US, where things are more bottom-up and depend on individual PIs chasing grants.

But I also want to be a bit careful here. There's a difference between AI for Science as a slogan and AI for Science as actual science. A lot of what gets labeled this way is really engineering, which is fine and valuable, like better protein structure prediction or faster molecular dynamics. But the thing I personally care most about is whether AI can help us discover new concepts, new laws, things that a human physicist would look at and say, "oh, I understand something I didn't understand before." That's much harder, and I don't think any country has really cracked it yet.

So my honest view is that China is very strong on the application side and on scale, and is catching up quickly on the fundamental side. What I'd love to see more of, both in China and everywhere, is people who are willing to work on the slower, more curiosity-driven questions. Interpretability, understanding why these models work, using physics ideas to understand AI itself. That's a smaller community, but I think that's where some of the most interesting ideas will come from in the long run.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a shift from using AI as a tool to using AI to improve the process of developing AI itself. Instead of researchers manually designing every component, we can ask which parts of experimentation, model design, and evaluation AI can help with.

In China, I think the opportunity is to connect that work with concrete problems. But I would distinguish between generating more experiments and generating more understanding. If AI helps us try a thousand ideas but we still don’t understand why one works, that’s useful, but it’s only part of the progress we want. The more interesting question is whether it can help us discover principles that make the next generation of models simpler, more reliable, and easier to understand.
